messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bank Teller
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 56

She is 30 years old, a married woman who works as a bank teller, and when she first begins telling her story, she does so in a careful, practiced way, as if speaking too freely might make something dangerous return. Before the trauma, her life is ordinary in the ways she now misses most. She and her husband rent a small apartment, argue lightly over groceries and laundry, and text each other during the day about dinner plans. At the bank, she likes the rhythm of the work: counting bills, greeting regular customers, balancing her drawer to the cent. She takes pride in being steady, polite, and dependable.

The change begins during a trip abroad two years earlier to visit a friend and do some traveling before trying to start a family. What happens there is something she circles around before saying plainly. She is detained by a group of men connected to local authorities after being in the wrong place during a political crackdown. She is held for several days in a concrete room with no window. She is bound, threatened, deprived of sleep, and repeatedly tortured. She remembers the scrape of a chair leg, the smell of damp cloth, the way one man hummed to himself while hurting her. More than the pain, she remembers the helplessness and the certainty, at several moments, that she will not survive.

She eventually comes home physically healed enough that other people assume the worst is over. In the first weeks back, she tells almost no one what happened. Even with her husband, she offers fragments. She says she was “mistreated,” then apologizes for being vague, then shuts down when he asks questions. At night she startles awake soaked in sweat, her heart pounding so hard she feels sick. In the dreams she is back in the room, unable to move or call out. Sometimes she wakes disoriented and pushes her husband away before recognizing where she is. He learns not to touch her suddenly in the dark.

As she returns to work at the bank, she tries to force herself into her old routines. She puts on makeup, ties back her hair, and stands behind the counter smiling at customers. For a while, this performance almost fools her. Then small things begin to break through. The click of the cash drawer sounds too much like metal striking metal. A man raising his voice about an overdraft sends a bolt of fear through her body so sharp that her fingers go numb. She loses track of a transaction mid-count and has to ask a customer to repeat himself, cheeks burning with shame. She begins scanning every person who enters, noting hands, posture, tone of voice, exits. By lunchtime she is exhausted from watching for danger in a place she once experienced as safe.

Outside of work, her life narrows. She avoids crowded stores, public transportation, and news reports about unrest or human rights abuses. She cannot tolerate being in a room with the door closed. In restaurants, she insists on sitting where she can see the entrance. Her husband notices that she no longer sings along to the radio in the car. She used to be quick with humor; now long silences stretch between them. He asks if she wants to visit friends, and she says she is tired. Often she is not tired exactly, but braced. Her body feels as if it never received the message that the danger ended.

What troubles her almost as much as fear is the change in how she sees herself. She thinks of herself as weak for having survived by complying, though another part of her knows she had no choice. She feels contaminated by the memories and ashamed of how often they intrude. There are whole afternoons at the bank when she appears composed while internally she is fighting off flashes of the room: the wall, the restraints, the voice of a man telling her no one will come. On those days she comes home and sits in the shower until the water runs cold. Her husband knocks gently and asks if she is all right, and she says yes because explaining feels impossible.

She sleeps lightly and listens for sounds in the hallway of the apartment building. If footsteps pause outside their door, her stomach clenches. She checks the lock repeatedly before bed, then lies awake replaying what she should have done differently on that trip, as if hindsight could rewrite it. Some mornings she cries before work in a way that feels detached, almost soundless, then wipes her face and goes in anyway. Her coworkers describe her as quiet now, more serious, though they still trust her because she never stops being conscientious.

In sessions, she speaks with the strained self-control of someone who has spent a long time containing terror so it will not spill into the room. She wants very much to be the woman she was before, the one who could stand at her station at the bank and think only about account numbers and polite conversation. Instead she lives with a constant sense of threat, a body that startles and recoils, a mind pulled backward into scenes she does not choose. She loves her husband and wants closeness with him, but often feels far away even while sitting beside him on the couch. What she mourns most is not only what was done to her, but how thoroughly it has altered the ordinary texture of her days.
